emphasize that the 16 key elements are interlinked and mutually reinforcing, and we recognize the critical relevance for the future strategic framework. We meet at a time when pressures on land are intensifying in every region. Desertification, land degradation, and drought, exacerbated by climate change, are already undermining food security, water availability, biodiversity, resilience, and livelihoods. The scale and urgency of these interconnected challenges call on us to act with clarity and ambition. This is why the Convention must equip itself with a robust, forward-looking and effective post-2030 strategic framework. It should help us to respond to emerging challenges, strengthen implementation and reinforce the relevance and impact of the Convention. We encourage strong and continuous involvement of Parties and stakeholders, including through regional consultation with parties and consultations with civil society, the private sector and practitioners. The group should also take into account relevant ongoing and forthcoming inputs, including work on monitoring and indicators, notably on gender and land tenure, lessons from the 2026 reporting process, the recommendation of the midterm evaluation of the 2018 to 2030 strategic framework and synergies with other multilateral monitoring frameworks. We further call for close coordination and synergies with the development of the post-2030 gender action plan. At the same time, the Futures Framework should remain flexible enough to reflect different national realities while ensuring that the indicator system is relevant, practical and workable for all parties. We also encourage the group to consider a comprehensive theory of change to help communicate the convention's impact. On ambition, future goals and targets should be science-based, implementation-oriented, and where possible, guided by smart principles. The post-2030 strategic framework should also strengthen proactive drought management while promoting science, gender equality, secure land tenure, and synergies with the Rio Conventions and other relevant global frameworks. The European Union and its Member States remain fully committed to working with all partners towards a strong, credible and effective post-2030 strategic framework. Thank you very much.

Thank you, Mr. Co-Chair. We thank you for convening this plenary session and for the opportunity to set our expectations for the future strategic framework of the convention. We meet at a moment when the challenges this convention was created to address are growing, not receding. Up to 40% of the world's land is already degraded and this directly affects around half of humanity. The frequency and intensity of droughts have risen by almost 30% since the year of 2000. And current projections indicate that by 2050, three in every four people may be affected by drought. If present trends continue, an additional area almost the size of South America could be degraded within that same period. It's precisely because the stakes are so high that Brazil attaches great importance to the work of the Intergovernmental Working Group of the Future Strategic Framework. Over three in-person sessions and under considerable time constraints, the group delivered a substantive report. We regret that this report could not be fully debated by parties at the session. Its value, however, remains. The group agreed on a shared vision for the post-2030 framework and identified the key elements that such framework should contain. That is a solid foundation. and one that reflects the priorities and perspectives of all regions. At the same time, we recognize that much remains to be done. The elements already identified must now be given more concrete, detailed and operational form, with clear recommendations, sound indicators and a credible approach to the means of implementation. The work cannot be improvised. It requires the continuation of the working group's mandate along the lines defined by decision four of COP16 in Riyadh so that the process keep its transparency, its inclusiveness and its foundation in consensus. Brazil therefore calls on delegations to support a pragmatic compromise solution that allows the working group to continue its work without interruption. Losing momentum would set back an effort that this convention and the people who depend on healthy land cannot afford to postpone. Mr. co-facilitator, Brazil wishes to be clear on the further point. This conference is convened to address the matters that fall within the mandate of this convention, namely desertification, land degradation, and drought, and those matters alone. Mr. Chair, on behalf of the Regional Implementation Annex for Central and Eastern Europe, I would like to address an issue for particular and growing importance to our region, drought. Our region includes countries with very diverse climatic, ecological, and socioeconomic conditions. Many of our countries have not traditionally been considered highly drought-prone. Yet, increasingly frequent and severe drought episodes are affecting agriculture, water resources, ecosystems, rural livelihoods and economies across Central and Eastern Europe. This experience reinforces a message that our region has raised for many years. Drought is a global challenge and should be addressed as such. It does not stop at national borders. nor is it confined to traditionally dry regions. Increasing drought impacts across Europe and other parts of the world demonstrate that preparedness and resilience are challenges for all countries. These trends are already visible across our region. For example, The declining water level of the Caspian Sea, the world's largest inland water body, with its accelerating pace, has far-reaching environmental, economic and social consequences, including contributing to desertification across the region, showing firsthand that the drought is indeed becoming a harsh reality of the region. While in Serbia, around 70% of 10.45 billion euros in weather and climate related losses between 2000 and 2024 was linked to drought and extreme temperatures, including at least 1 billion euros in losses in summer 2024 alone. We recognize the important progress achieved under the convention, including the development of national drought plans, monitoring and early warning tools, knowledge platforms and regional cooperation mechanisms. However, planning alone is not sufficient. The priority now must be implementation. National drought plans need to be translated into concrete actions, investment strategies and projects. Countries need stronger institutional and technical capacities, functioning monitoring and early warning systems, Improved for many countries in our region, particularly those with limited institutional and financial capacities, this remained a significant constraint. Regional cooperation is equally important. Meteorological, agricultural and hydrological drought do not respect borders. Shared water resources, monitoring networks, scientific knowledge and experience provide strong reasons to strengthen regional and sub-regional cooperation as an operational part of drought resilience. Annex V therefore believes that a meaningful outcome on drought is in high demand and recognise the enormous work done to address drought under the UNCCD. We believe it will be a strong basement for the COP18 to make strong commitments to enhance drought resilience and ensure well-being of our communities. We recognize the different views among parties regarding the eventual form of the global drought arrangement, as well as the realities of the current international context. At the same time, these differences should be solved on the basis of consensus. Our region is therefore ready to explore a voluntary country-driven approach that can initiate stronger global cooperation on drought, while allowing that cooperation to evolve over time. The experience of land degradation neutrality demonstrates that voluntary national objectives and targets can create political momentum, improve national coordination, mobilize investment, and progressively strengthen implementation. A similar approach could be explored for drought resilience. Parties could, according to their national circumstances and capacities, voluntarily establish drought resilience objectives, targets or milestones supported by national drought plans, monitoring and early warning systems, regional cooperation, science, capacity building and access to finance. Such an approach would make maximum use of existing UNCCD institutions, mechanisms and tools, avoid unnecessary additional reporting burdens, and focus on measurable progress and implementation on the ground. Importantly, taking practical action now does not need to prejudge the future. Progress could be reviewed at a future session of the Conference of the Parties, allowing parties to consider whether further measures, institutional arrangements, or strengthened forms of international cooperation are required. We believe that this provides a possible bridge between urgency and political reality. Annex V stands ready for further constructive cooperation with all parties towards a future meaningful decision within the UNCCD that will strengthen proactive drought management and leave the door open for greater ambition in the future. Our objective should be clear, move from plans to implementation. from reaction to preparedness and from fragmented national responses to stronger cooperation on a challenge that is truly global. Thank you, Mr. Chair.

We also call for direct financing, accessible sustained funding for locally led land restoration and drought resilience initiative. land degradation neutrality, stronger implementation through inclusive national partnerships, ecosystem investments, funding for climate mitigation and adaptation, agroecology, agroforestry, water management and soil health across stable and conflict affected regions, grassroots capacity building that is empowerment to extending directly to community led actors, and inclusive science policy integration, reporting mechanisms that combine scientific evidence with traditional and local knowledge. We also call for people-centered post-2030 strategy, bottom-up governance driven by rights holders, anticipatory drought resilience, shifting from reactive management to proactive locally informed actions, women's leadership, full participation of women, including indigenous and pastoralist women in land governance, equitable land tenure that is secure land access and rights for women, vulnerable groups and local populations as a foundation for justice. And we know that solutions already exist in communities worldwide. The challenge is ensuring political will, financing solutions, and accountability match the urgency of the crisis. We call for the COP17 to be remembered for protecting saving space, honouring traditional knowledge, and renewing our commitment to healthy land. History will judge us by the landscape restored and communities empowered. The land and its people cannot wait. The time is now for transformative action and we are here to implement it. Thank you, Madam Chair.

Thank you very much. Dear delegates, I'm speaking on behalf of the UNCCD Youth Caucus. We young people from communities and region across the world come to COP17 with a shared message. The future of our land is the future of our generation. The following core messages reflect a direct call from young people worldwide to the delegates, ministers and leaders gathered at COP17. First, Institutionalize youth participation. Ensure young people are formally involved throughout national UNCCD processes, from policy design and implementation to monitoring and evaluation, including national action programs and land degradation neutrality strategies. Two, fully implement the youth engagement strategy. Move the youth engagement strategy from a global framework to practical national and regional action through clear implementation guidance, sharing of good practices and integration into relevant policies and programmes. Direct resources to frontline youth. Provide accessible non-debt funding such as dedicated grants and small grants alongside technical support, mentorship and capacity building. Funding should minimize bureaucracy and be accessible to youth-led and local-led organizations. Four, recognize land as a living system. Treat land as interconnected with food, water, biodiversity, health, livelihoods, culture and peace. Prioritize holistic landscape management, regenerative agriculture, and soil health over short-term extraction. Five, protect pastoralism and local knowledge. Recognize pastoralism, rangeland stewardship, and indigenous and local land practices as effective restoration approaches. Measure restoration by genuine ecosystem recovery rather than simplistic indicators such as tree planting numbers. Six, build stronger government youth partnerships. Treat youth organizations as implementation partners by creating regular dialogue and collaboration across governments, civil society, academia, and private sector. Strengthen pathways for young people to access knowledge, education, and careers in land restoration and sustainable land management. 7. Expand capacity building and intergenerational learning. Equip young people with the skills, knowledge and networks needed to participate meaningfully in UNCCD processes and turn commitments into action, including through training on negotiations, policies, sustainable land management and implementation. 8. Measure and strengthen accountability for youth engagements. Make youth participation measurable through voluntary reporting and indicators that assess both its quantity and quality. Track whether youth people, young people actually influence decisions, implementation, monitoring and evaluation, not simply whether they attend meetings. And last, nine, strengthen youth coordination within the UNCCD Secretariat. Consider establishing a dedicated youth focal point within the Secretariat to improve communication between the Secretariat, parties and youth organization. Expand access to opportunities and information and support the implementation of the youth engagement strategy. Thank you.

Thank you, Chair, distinguished delegates. We Indigenous peoples from the seven socio-cultural regions of the world have come to COP17 as the custodians, guardians and knowledge holders of the lands and territories that this convention seeks to protect and restore. But we must begin by expressing our deep disappointment that the agenda of this COP has removed the dedicated space for Indigenous peoples. the very peoples who have protected and sustained these lands and ecosystems for generations. We cannot restore the land while removing the voices of those who care for it. At COP16 in Riyadh, we celebrated together the adoption of decision 5/COP.16, establishing the Indigenous Peoples Caucus within the UNCCD. That was a major step forward. We call on you to uphold your commitments as we are upholding ours and we thank those who stand beside us. During People's Day, Indigenous peoples came together at the high-level special event, From Sacred Lands to Shepherding the Future, where we shared our realities, knowledge, solutions and adopted our Indigenous Peoples' Declaration. We call on parties to recognize this declaration and ensure that its priorities are reflected in the work and outcomes of this convention. This must not remain a statement from indigenous people. It must become a commitment followed by implementation. Our message is simple. There can be no meaningful land restoration without respect for the rights of the peoples who care for the land. We call on parties to recognize our collective land and territorial rights, customary governance, self-determination, and free, prior, and informed consent. We also call for science not to replace Indigenous peoples' knowledge, however, to stand alongside us. We remind parties that Indigenous pastoralism and the mobilities must be protected, including Indigenous women and youth. Finally, we call for direct, flexible and equitable and accessible finance to reach indigenous peoples and indigenous led organizations without unnecessary barriers or intermediaries. COP16 opened the door. COP17 must walk through it. And we stand ready to work together as partners towards COP18 to ensure that this is not only about creating a space for us to speak, it is about ensuring that we have a place where decisions are made about us and our territories. So today, we call on parties to move from recognition to implementation, from promises to action, from sacred lands to shepherding the future. We do not come only with demands, we come with solutions, for our lands, our territories, our knowledge and our future. Thank you.

Thank you, Madam Chair. Ministerial dialogue innovative financial mechanisms for healthy land and drought resilience. This ministerial dialogue was officially opened and chaired by Mr. Togmid Dorjkhund, Deputy Prime Minister of Mongolia, representing the COP17 presidency, highlighting the significant finance gap for addressing land degradation and desertification, and placing investment and finance at the heart of the COP17 deliberations. Keynote remarks were made by the Deputy Secretary General of the United Nations, Ms. Amina J. Mohammed, and the Executive Secretary of the United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification, Ms. Yasemin ****. These opening remarks framed land not only as an environmental concern but as the economic infrastructure underpinning food, water, jobs, public revenue and stability. Because when land fails, the conditions are borne by the state treasury through increased subsidies, emergency relief, displacement and security deployments. The speakers called for repurposing of agricultural subsidies alongside incentives such as environmental taxes, payments for ecosystem services and debt instruments, for portfolios with sufficient skills underpinned by revenue models with multiple benefits, risk sharing and local currency financing and for the conversion of national drought plans into drought investment plans and the integration of land finance across the Rio conventions. The chair opened the next segment by announcing the launch of the rangelands flagship initiative as a key pillar of Mongolia's legacy as a COP17 president. The initiative seeks to mobilize resources for sustainable rangeland management and restoration and establish a country-led coalition of rangeland states. It also aims to create the Eurasian Center for the Climate Resilient Drylands as a regional hub for science, innovation, and investment. Mongolia committed to a sector-wide sustainable finance principles, a green taxonomy, and a target of 10% green lending by 2030. Other stakeholders including the Asian Development Bank, the African Development Bank, the International Union for the Conservation of Nature, Luxembourg, Spain, Germany, and the European Union all announced new financial commitments in the support of the UNCCD related projects and programs spanning drought resilience, ecosystem based adaptation, food system resilience, and the restoration of dryland landscapes. Overall, the dialogue welcomed pledges totaling $1.3 billion, including the Rangeland Flagship Initiative portfolio of over 45 projects worth $1.2 billion. This was followed by a moderated discussion with ministerial representatives of Brazil, the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, South Africa, and the People's Republic of China, as well as high level participants from the World Bank, the European Investment Bank, the World Economic Forum, and that explored why land remains outside mainstream budgets and portfolios despite a strong investment case. Participants noted that the binding constraints on the greater investment are often mandates, instruments, pipeline, or risk appetite. They underline that treating land as a capital asset requires making restoration bankable, improving revenue visibility, and providing policy certainty, stressing the need to reflect on how public and concessional finance can be most effectively deployed. Over 60 parties and 10 representatives of international organizations then delivered statements during the full day dialogue. Most speakers refer to the UNCCD financial needs assessment for the 139 country parties and over 350 national action plans, which estimates that 355 billion US dollars are required annually up to 2030 against the current investment of 77 billion, representing an annual gap of 278 billion. Set against an estimated 878 billion a year in losses from inaction, the investment case was presented as a one, eight to one return with potential benefits of 1.8 trillion US dollars a year. The cost of inaction was put at three times the cost of restoration. Many speakers noted that the significant contraction in the official development assistance in 2025 and that roughly half of the low-income countries are at risk of debt distress. There is consensus that the finance needed for sustainable land management cannot be delivered through grants alone. This discussion turned on how countries tax, spend, and borrow, whether public resources crowd in private capital rather than substitute for it. Many parties indicated that how they prioritize domestic fiscal measures in the form of incentives. public private blended finance and the repurposing of environmentally harmful subsidies. Several parties called for the simplified access to multilateral funds, shorter turnaround times for approval and greater coherence across the land, climate and biodiversity financing windows. They urge multilateral development banks to establish a distinct trackable, category for land, soil health, and drought resilience within the existing nature and climate finance taxonomies. This call was based on the principle that what is not measured is not allocated. There is a broad support for the innovative financing mechanisms, scaling guarantees, force loss capital, and index-based insurance. Others caution that the innovative finance must not become a means of transferring the responsibilities of states to private actors. Some parties stress the need to mobilize private sector investment alongside public finance, as well as the important role of capacity building, cooperation, and technology transfer for effective implementation of land and water management practices including affordable digital and satellite technologies. Several voiced the need for project preparation support to develop an investment ready pipeline and for a shift from small and fragmented projects to investable programs portfolios. They also cautioned against the widening access gaps for the least developed countries and those in fragile contexts. Sovereign instruments, debt for nature swaps, Nature performance bonds, sustainable link bonds, and country platforms were raised as the unfinished business of the severe commitment. Parties called for simple, flexible, predictable, and equitable access to finance for land-based initiatives, especially for developing and landlocked countries and small island developing states. Speakers urged that indigenous peoples, local communities, and pastoralists be engaged as economic partners rather than as beneficiaries. Ministerial dialogue drove resilience. The ministerial dialogue was opened and chaired by Ms. Sandagocher Sen, Minister of Environment and Climate Change of Mongolia, representing the COP17 presidency. Opening remarks were delivered by Mr. Nomtobaia Namisder, Deputy Prime Minister of Mongolia, who announced the Water Land Nexus Initiative, a Mongolia-led global initiative with the step action agenda aimed at advancing integrated science-based and finance-ready solutions to interconnected water and land challenges. The initiative seeks to strengthen drought resilience through regional cooperation and improve soil moisture and landscape water retention. Miss Amina J. Mohammed, Deputy Secretary General of the United Nations, and Miss Yasmin Ford, Executive Secretary of the UNCCD, delivered keynote remarks, underscoring the increasing frequency and severity of drought, its far-reaching impacts, and the high cost of inaction. They call for a shift from reactive crisis response to proactive drought resilience and stronger collective action, pointing at the International Drought Resilience Alliance, IDRA, in strengthening international cooperation and the International Drought Resilience Observatory, IDRO, in advancing drought data, science and knowledge, as well as the Drought Resilience Investment Facility, DRIF. and the Global Drought Resilience Partnership and the Global Environment Facility that are mobilizing finance and investment for drought resilience. They stressed the urgent need priority to operationalize these initiatives and translate available resources, knowledge and partnerships into concrete action at national and local levels. Professor James Flamigetti highlighted unprecedented continental drying, shrinking freshwater availability and the importance of accessible science and data to support effective decision making and policy responses. a ministerial panel brought together by representatives of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, France, the United Arab Emirates, Arab Republic of Egypt, Luxembourg and Spain to strengthen the political will and to raise awareness of the drought as a global challenge that requires mobilizing finance at scale, accelerating ecosystem restoration and strengthening collaboration from the global to the local level, including transboundary cooperation. They also underscored the need to move towards proactive drought management, pointing to the effectiveness of the water use restrictions and increased efficiencies, while also stressing the importance of early warning, science and data, and integrated approaches, including nature-based solutions. These include preparedness-based approaches, focus on managing water scarcity through smart distribution and drip irrigation, supported by modern technologies and the development of new water resources. All stressed that whole of government and the whole of society approaches are essential to overcome silos. A technical panel with senior representatives from the African Union, United Habitat, ESCAP, UNESCO, the World Group discusses drought implications for global trade supply chains and economic resilience they emphasize the urgent need to shift from crisis financing to resilience investment that requires stronger cross-sectional collaboration with due consideration for urban rural linkages They also pointed out two examples of regional cooperation that combined satellite data, ground observations, and seasonal forecasting to strengthen early warning and anticipatory action. All agreed that water is a human right and drew attention to the disproportionate impacts of drought on women and girls, including increased workloads, loss of livelihoods, and reduced access to essential resources. Over 60 parties together with representatives of international organizations and civil society organizations delivered statements. Speakers echoed the priorities highlighted by the keynotes and the panelists while adding read national and regional perspectives, recognizing drought as a structural challenge rather than a temporary shortage of water, with cascading impacts on the ecosystems, people, livelihoods and economies, and the growing implications for security stability, including involuntary migration. They call for proactive drought management and for a placing of land water nexus at the heart of collective action. recognizing that protecting and restoring land is essential to safeguarding water resources. They highlighted the need to break down policy silos and strengthen integration across sectors and plans to combat climate change, biodiversity loss, and land degradation. Many speakers acknowledged the availability of proven measures, including improved water use efficiency, strengthening groundwater management, expanding water use and recycling, modernizing irrigation, promoting rainwater harvesting and sustainable soil management, advancing climate resilient agriculture and improved crop and livestock varieties, and restoring ecosystems and landscapes, including through afforestation and nature-based solutions. Several interventions emphasize the need for stronger global, regional, and transboundary cooperation, including south-south cooperation to facilitate the transfer of knowledge, experience, technologies, and solutions. Most parties call for predictive and anticipatory financing and insurance, as well as innovative and blended finance mechanisms, particularly in vulnerable countries and communities. This includes the alignment of drought resilience with the development and climate finance, mobilizing private sector investment, strengthening partnership with financial institutions, and making financing directly accessible to people and communities that is inclusive and responsive to the needs of rural communities, including families and children, women, youth, farmers, indigenous peoples, and pastoralists. Ministerial dialogue restoration of rangelands and well-being of pastoralist communities. This dialogue was opened by the COP president and was chaired by Botswana and Uruguay with keynote remarks from Ms. Inga Andersen, executive director of the United Nations Environment Program and Ms. Beth Cole, direct deputy director general of the food and agricultural organization in the United Nations. They emphasize the importance of range lands for food security, regional economic development, and the livelihoods and cultures of pastoralists who steward these vast landscapes. While range lands provide 16% of global food production and 70% of feed for livestock, they host abundant biodiversity, sequester carbon and contribute to water cycles. Despite their significant environmental and socioeconomic value, rangelands are often overlooked and undervalued in national economies. Over 52 parties and 10 representatives of international organizations delivered statements. Virtually all agreed that rangelands must be recognized, respected, and restored. Healthy rangelands ensure that ecological integrity is maintained, which is critical to feed a growing population and to achieve land restoration, biodiversity conservation, and climate change mitigation and adaptation targets. Many acknowledge that the growing pressures on rangelands and their communities from urban development, energy generation, mining, and high intensity agriculture, as well as the effects of rapid climate change, accelerating land degradation and recurring droughts. They recognize that the policies and regulations to govern rangelands must ensure healthy and productive rangelands for future generations. Rangelands must be explicitly reflected in national strategies and action plans for ecosystem conservation, land restoration, and sustainable grazing that promote well-managed ecological pastoralism as a sustainable economic development model. Several parties emphasize the importance of traditional knowledge systems and the empowerment of pastoralists local communities and the indigenous peoples to actively participate and take on leadership in the planning, management and governance of rangelands. Responsibility and inclusive, responsible and inclusive land governance such as ensuring tenure security and women's lands rights were identified as critical enabling factors. They also highlighted the importance of integrated land use planning that considers pastoral mobility and resource access as part of the adaptation strategy and to ensure social stability, dignity and peace. The mapping and monitoring of rangeland health and the use of digital technologies to assess potential degradation processes was highlighted as an important pillar in the sustainable rangeland management. While all speakers welcome the Rangelands Flagship Initiative and the Coalition of Rangeland States, many emphasize considerable investments required to conserve, sustainably manage, and restore rangelands. Some speakers called on the global community to provide financial resources to create an enabling environment through technical assistance, technology transfer, sharing of best practices. and to facilitate greater sustainable and inclusive investments in rangelands. Some pointed to sustainable value chains that can incentivize stewardship and significantly improve the livelihoods and well-being of pastoralist communities. This includes enhanced access to markets and inputs for pastoralists and agro-pastoralist communities to support their traditional livelihoods that are based on extensive livestock production systems. It was acknowledged that the International Year of Rangelands and Pastoralists has raised the profile of rangelands and their role in safeguarding planetary stability. Many parties emphasize the need to move from commitments to action by driving inclusive policy frameworks and governance systems, responsible investments, and building on rich heritage and vast traditional knowledge of pastoralists and the rangeland communities who have managed these dynamic landscapes for centuries. Thank you.
